newsitem.title: RUSSIA: N.Korean envoy says Kim succession expected soon.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean envoy says Kim succession expected soon.

text.p: North Korea's envoy in Moscow said he was sure the country's effective ruler Kim Jong-il, son of late "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung, would formally assume top state positions soon, Itar-Tass news agency reported on Wednesday.

"Kim Jong-il, undoubtedly, is our leader without any elections or appointments," Tass quoted ambassador Son Song Pil as saying. "I think he will be elevated to the top positions, but there have been no decisions on when and in what form."

He added he expected the decision to be taken soon because the three-year mourning for Kim Il-sung, who ruled his Stalinist state with an iron hand for more than four decades, formally ended on Tuesday.
Earlier this month, the ambassador, who is a senior figure in the North Korean hiearchy, hinted Kim Jong-il could be appointed as supreme leader of the party and state as soon as the mourning ended.
Since the death of his father on July 8, 1994, Kim Jong-il, now 55, has established full personal control but the formal top party post and the state presidency have been left vacant.

Western political analysts have said there are no indications North Korea is preparing a succession ceremony for Kim Jong-il and suggested the actual dynastic succession was not likely to occur in the next few months.

The ambassador said there would be no changes to the course of the ruling Communist Party and said he expected no big reshuffle in the North Korean leadership, although he hinted some elderly officials could be relieved of their duties.
"There may be no changes in the course and in the line of the leadership. We will be following the line and the course defined by comrade Kim Il-sung," he said.

"Those who have been true to the line and the course of comrade Kim Il-sung will retain their positions...excluding those who are physically unable to perform their duties, for example due to their old age."
Tass also quoted a Russian Foreign Ministry official as saying Russia was preparing to send food aid to famine-threatened North Korea.

"The situation in North Korea is very difficult now, above all there is the food problem," the official said. "But there is no dramatic state of affairs there, no social chaos. The state keeps functioning."

International aid officials say many North Koreans are near starvation and could die in the next few months unless food arrives. Food is being shipped to North Korea by Christian organisations and volunteers.

Russian leftists, in a Soviet-style gesture of international solidarity, said earlier in June they planned to collect food for famine-threatened North Korea under the slogan "A kilo of rice for a Korean friend".
North Korea was a long-time ally of the now-defunct Soviet Union but ties with Russia are less solid because Moscow has turned increasingly to other countries, including South Korea.
